title: What Is a PPO? How PPO Health Plans Work
summary: What is a PPO? Learn how PPO health insurance plans work, what they cost, and how a PPO compares with HMO, EPO, and HDHP plans before you choose coverage.
body_markdown:
If you're comparing health insurance plans during open enrollment, you've almost certainly seen the acronym PPO. A PPO, or preferred provider organization, is a health plan that lets you see in-network and out-of-network providers without a referral, in exchange for higher monthly premiums. This guide explains what a PPO is, how PPO costs work, and how a PPO plan compares with other plan types.


## What does PPO stand for and how does it work?


PPO stands for preferred provider organization. A PPO is a type of health insurance plan built around a contracted network of preferred doctors, hospitals, clinics, and other health care providers.[HealthCare.gov](https://www.healthcare.gov/glossary/preferred-provider-organization-ppo/) describes it as a plan where you pay less if you use providers in the plan's network, and you can use doctors, hospitals, and providers outside the network for an additional cost. PPOs are offered through employers, the ACA Health Insurance Marketplace, and directly from private insurers. They're the most common employer plan: 46% of covered workers were enrolled in a PPO in 2025, according to the[KFF 2025 Employer Health Benefits Survey](https://www.kff.org/health-costs/2025-employer-health-benefits-survey/) .


Here's the basic mechanic: insurers negotiate discounted rates with in-network providers. When you visit a network provider, you pay lower costs through smaller copays or coinsurance, because the plan has pre-negotiated those rates on your behalf. Our guide to[in-network vs. out-of-network care](https://www.withflex.com/blog/in-network-vs-out-of-network) explains networks in more detail.


PPO plans cover visits to both in-network and out-of-network providers. If you see an out-of-network provider, you keep your coverage but pay a larger share of the bill, often through a separate, higher deductible and steeper coinsurance. You may also need to submit claims yourself.


A practical example: if you visit a dermatologist inside the PPO network, you might owe a flat $30 copay. Visit the same dermatologist out of network, and you could owe 40% of the allowed amount plus any balance-billed amount above the plan's allowed rate.


PPO plans typically don't require you to pick a primary care physician, and you don't need a referral to see a specialist. That makes a PPO a good fit for people who want the freedom to choose and switch doctors without extra paperwork. The flexibility comes at a price: PPO health plans usually carry higher monthly premiums than more restrictive plans.


## Key features of PPO health insurance plans


Here's what sets PPO insurance apart from other health plan types:


- **No PCP requirement.** You don't need to select a primary care provider or route all care through one doctor.
- **No referral requirement.** You can schedule specialist visits directly.
- **In-network and out-of-network access.** PPO plans cover both, giving you more flexibility than most other types of health plans.
- **Large network reach.** PPO networks are often broad and can span multiple states, which helps families, frequent travelers, and people who split time across regions.
- **Emergency care coverage.** Like other ACA-compliant plans, a PPO can't charge you more in copays or coinsurance for emergency care at an out-of-network hospital, and it can't require prior approval for emergency room services,[according to HealthCare.gov](https://www.healthcare.gov/using-marketplace-coverage/getting-emergency-care/) .
- **Specialist and facility breadth.** A typical PPO network includes specialists in cardiology, orthopedics, behavioral health, women's health, and other services, plus hospitals and outpatient facilities.
- **Dental PPOs.** Many insurers also offer dental PPO (DPPO) plans that work the same way: no primary dentist requirement and discounted rates with in-network dentists.


During[open enrollment](https://www.withflex.com/blog/your-2026-open-enrollment-cheat-sheet-7-terms-you-actually-need-to-know) , review each plan's Summary of Benefits and Coverage to confirm how your PPO handles covered services, preventive care, and cost sharing.


## Costs of a PPO: premiums, deductibles, and trade-offs


The central trade-off with a PPO health plan is straightforward: you pay higher monthly[premiums](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-a-premium) in exchange for broader provider choice and out-of-network access. PPO premiums are typically higher than those for HMO or EPO plans from the same insurer or employer.


Beyond the premium, PPO plans use several layers of cost sharing:


- **Deductible.** Many PPOs have separate[deductibles](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-a-deductible) for in-network and out-of-network care. You pay the full allowed cost of most non-preventive care until you meet it.
- **Copays.** A flat fee per visit, such as $25 for a primary care visit. Learn more about[how copays work](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-a-copay) .
- **Coinsurance.** A percentage of the bill you owe after meeting your deductible, often around 20% in network and higher out of network. See[how coinsurance works](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-coinsurance) .
- **Out-of-pocket maximum.** The most you pay for covered in-network care in a plan year. For 2026, the ACA limit is $10,600 for self-only coverage and $21,200 for family coverage ([HealthCare.gov](https://www.healthcare.gov/glossary/out-of-pocket-maximum-limit/) ). Once you reach it, the plan pays 100% of covered in-network care for the rest of the year. Our guide to the[deductible vs. out-of-pocket maximum](https://www.withflex.com/blog/deductible-vs-out-of-pocket-maximum) shows how the two fit together.


Out-of-pocket costs can climb when you use out-of-network providers. Out-of-network doctors can balance-bill you for the difference between their charge and what the plan considers the allowed amount, though the[No Surprises Act](https://www.cms.gov/nosurprises/ending-surprise-medical-bills) protects you in emergencies and certain other situations. Out-of-network spending may also not count toward your in-network out-of-pocket maximum. And even without referrals, some procedures under a PPO may require prior authorization.


One more note: a traditional PPO usually isn't a high-deductible health plan (HDHP), which is the type of plan required to contribute to a Health Savings Account. Some PPO-network plans are built as HDHPs. For 2026, an HSA-qualified HDHP must have a deductible of at least $1,700 for self-only coverage or $3,400 for family coverage ([IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-19](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/rp-25-19.pdf) ). Our[PPO vs. HDHP comparison](https://www.withflex.com/blog/ppo-vs-hdhp) covers the trade-offs.


## How PPOs compare with other health insurance plan types


Many people choose between a PPO, a health maintenance organization (HMO), an exclusive provider organization (EPO), a point of service (POS) plan, or a high-deductible health plan. Here's how they differ:


- **PPO vs. HMO.**[HMO plans](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-an-hmo) require in-network providers for non-emergency care, usually require a primary care provider, and need referrals to see specialists. HMOs usually have lower monthly premiums but offer less flexibility. See our full[HMO vs. PPO comparison](https://www.withflex.com/blog/hmo-vs-ppo) .
- **PPO vs. EPO.** An EPO generally doesn't require referrals but won't cover out-of-network providers except for emergency care. EPOs tend to cost less than PPOs because of tighter network rules. More in our[EPO vs. PPO guide](https://www.withflex.com/blog/epo-vs-ppo) .
- **PPO vs. POS.** Point of service plans blend HMO-style PCP and referral rules with some out-of-network coverage. POS out-of-network access is typically narrower than a full PPO's.
- **PPO vs. HDHP.** HDHPs must meet IRS minimum deductible and maximum out-of-pocket limits and can be paired with an HSA. They often have lower premiums but higher upfront costs before coverage kicks in.


A Medicare Advantage plan labeled as a PPO works on similar principles but follows Medicare-specific rules. Always confirm features in your specific plan documents. Labels alone don't guarantee identical network rules, referral policies, or cost structures.


### PPO vs. HMO and EPO: network rules at a glance


- **HMO.** Coverage limited to in-network providers (except emergencies). Requires a PCP. Referrals needed for specialists.
- **EPO.** In-network care only (except emergencies). Usually no PCP or referral requirement.
- **PPO.** In-network and out-of-network care without referrals. Out-of-network care costs more and may involve more paperwork, such as submitting your own claims.


## Who might benefit from a PPO plan, and how HSAs and FSAs fit in


The right insurance plan depends on your health needs, provider preferences, and budget. A PPO may suit people who:


- See multiple specialists and want direct access without referrals
- Have preferred doctors who are sometimes out of network
- Live in or travel across multiple states
- Have family members managing chronic conditions who need a range of health care services


During open enrollment, list your preferred doctors and hospitals, then check whether they're in network under each plan you're considering. That single step can prevent surprise bills later.


Tax-advantaged accounts can work alongside PPO coverage. A[Flexible Spending Account](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-are-hsas-fsas) lets you set aside pre-tax dollars for qualified medical expenses under IRS rules, such as deductibles, copays, and prescriptions, and employers often offer one alongside a PPO. A Health Savings Account requires enrollment in an HSA-qualified HDHP, so it's only an option if your PPO-network plan is built as one.


Understanding how a PPO works, including its network rules, cost layers, and trade-offs, puts you in a stronger position when choosing coverage. Review your plan's Summary of Benefits and Coverage, confirm your providers are in network, and compare total yearly costs, not just premiums.
